item.title: PELICAN: keeping cardiac index at each patient's own baseline did not cut 7-day complications; 90-day death doubled
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2026-10-19

Multicenter European RCT of 1,111 high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery: an algorithm of crystalloid boluses and dobutamine held intraoperative cardiac index at or above the patient's preoperative resting value, versus routine hemodynamic management with the same MAP target.

Take-home

  • Composite of AKI, myocardial injury, severe infection, cardiac arrest or death at 7 days: 44.3% vs 46.9%, not different
  • Dobutamine ran in 64% of intervention patients versus 0.5% of controls; 90-day mortality 5.7% vs 2.8% (exploratory)
  • Personalized cardiac index targets with routine inotrope support should not be adopted; keep MAP above 65 and give fluid for a reason

Why it matters. Goal-directed hemodynamic therapy has been argued over for two decades; OPTIMISE and OPTIMISE II were neutral or nearly so. The newer idea was to personalize the target: keep each patient's cardiac index at the value they had awake and resting, rather than maximizing stroke volume. PELICAN is the first large trial of that approach.

What they did. Saugel and colleagues randomized 1,111 patients aged 45 or older with at least one high-risk criterion having elective major visceral abdominal surgery of 90 minutes or more, at 12 university centers in five European countries (2023 to 2025). Cardiac index was measured noninvasively in everyone. The intervention arm used balanced crystalloid at 6 mL/kg/h, 500 mL boluses and dobutamine to hold cardiac index at or above the preoperative resting value; controls got usual care with the display blinded. Both arms targeted MAP above 65 mm Hg.

What they found. The primary composite of AKI, myocardial injury, severe infection, nonfatal cardiac arrest or death within 7 days occurred in 44.3% vs 46.9% (relative risk 0.94, 95.1% CI 0.83 to 1.08). No component differed; AKI was 9.6% vs 13.0%. The protocol worked as designed: median cardiac index 3.1 vs 2.7 L/min/m2, dobutamine in 64.1% vs 0.5%. Hospital stay was a day shorter (8 vs 9). The uncomfortable finding is 90-day mortality: 5.7% vs 2.8% (RR 2.06, 1.13 to 3.78), an exploratory secondary outcome not adjusted for multiplicity.

Caveats. Single-blind, one surgical population, and a mortality signal that could be chance; the trial cannot say whether dobutamine, extra fluid or something else drove it.

For anesthesiologists. Chasing a personalized cardiac index with routine dobutamine is not supported and may be harmful. Cardiac output monitoring remains useful for working out why a patient is hypotensive; treating the number for its own sake is not.

item.title: Surgical bailout during TAVR fell to 0.4% of 400,000 Medicare cases, but 26% of bailed-out patients die within 30 days
item.description:
JACC Cardiovasc Interv · Registry · 2026-09-14

A CMS analysis of 400,862 TAVR procedures from 2016 to 2024 finds same-day open surgery in 0.56% overall, halving over the period, with 30-day mortality of 26.3% versus 1.8% and no improvement in bailout mortality over time.

Take-home

  • Bailout fell from 0.92% in 2016 to 0.40% in 2024: hematoma evacuation 38%, ventricular repair 20%, SAVR 16%, CABG 13%, aortic 11%
  • Mortality after bailout 26.3% at 30 days, 35% at one year, 48% at five years, versus 1.8%, 10% and 26% without
  • Thirty-day death was 41% when SAVR was combined with other repairs versus 19% for isolated SAVR; institutional SAVR volume made no difference

Why it matters. The US national coverage determination for TAVR no longer requires on-site cardiac surgery in the way it once did, and the solo TAVR operator is being argued for in print. This is the largest contemporary look at what happens when a transfemoral valve goes wrong. Braasch and colleagues published it in JACC: Cardiovascular Interventions (19:2364-2375, September 2026) with two opposing editorials.

What they did. Every Medicare TAVR from January 2016 to December 2024, 400,862 procedures, with surgical bailout defined as any open cardiac operation on the same day.

What they found.

  • Bailout in 2,240 patients, 0.56% overall, falling from 0.92% in 2016 to 0.40% in 2024.
  • Procedures: mediastinal hematoma evacuation 38%, ventricular repair 20%, SAVR 16%, CABG 13%, aortic surgery 11%.
  • Mortality with versus without bailout: 26.3% versus 1.8% at 30 days, 35% versus 10% at one year, 48% versus 26% at five years. Early mortality did not fall over the study period. Patients who survived the first year had long-term outcomes comparable to those who never needed surgery.
  • Thirty-day mortality was 41% when SAVR was combined with other interventions and 19% for isolated SAVR. Institutional SAVR volume did not change the odds: 27%, 29% and 25% across low, intermediate and high-volume centers.

Caveats. Administrative data cannot say why each bailout happened or how the decision was made, and a same-day operation misses rescue surgery on day two.

For the anesthesiologist. One in roughly 250 TAVRs still ends in an open chest, and three in four of those patients survive the first month. The editorials split on what that means for surgical standby; for the anesthesia team it means the cannulation plan, blood, and a perfusionist's phone number belong in every TAVR briefing, however routine the case looks.

item.title: MIST: multivessel CABG through a small thoracotomy beat sternotomy on 1-month physical recovery, with no deaths or strokes
item.description:
Lancet · RCT · 2026-07-31

An investigator-initiated, open-label randomised trial at seven centres in six countries assigned 170 patients with multivessel coronary disease to minimally invasive CABG via a small thoracotomy or conventional sternotomy; the primary endpoint was patient-reported physical recovery (SF-36 physical component) at one month.

Take-home

  • SF-36 physical component at 1 month: 45.1 vs 42.2, a 2.9-point gain for minimally invasive CABG (p=0.031).
  • No deaths or strokes through 12 months in either arm; one early major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event with the minimally invasive approach.
  • Experienced teams and selected patients; expect more one-lung ventilation, thoracotomy analgesia and peripheral cannulation in CABG rooms.

Why it matters. Minimally invasive multivessel CABG through a small left thoracotomy has spread on the promise of faster recovery, but until now the randomised evidence against sternotomy was thin. MIST is the first international randomised comparison with a patient-centred primary outcome.

What they did. Ruel, Nambala, Guo and colleagues randomised 170 patients with multivessel coronary artery disease 1:1 to minimally invasive CABG (86) or sternotomy CABG (84) at seven centres in six countries (NCT03447938). The trial was open-label; the primary endpoint was physical recovery at one month measured by the SF-36 physical component summary, with safety followed to 12 months. Funding came from Medtronic.

What they found.

  • One-month SF-36 physical component: 45.1 with minimally invasive CABG versus 42.2 with sternotomy, a mean difference of 2.9 points (95% CI 0.3 to 5.5; p=0.031).
  • No deaths and no strokes in either group through 12 months.
  • One major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event occurred in the minimally invasive group before one month.

Caveats. The trial is small, the outcome is patient-reported in an unblinded design, the centres were experienced minimally invasive programs with selected patients, and a 2.9-point SF-36 difference is modest. Long-term graft patency is not addressed here. The authors themselves call for implementation and longer-term studies.

For the anesthesiologist. If your surgeons take this up, the anesthetic changes more than the incision: lung isolation and one-lung ventilation during grafting, often with a double-lumen tube, TEE support for positioning and de-airing where cardiopulmonary bypass or peripheral cannulation is used, thoracotomy-appropriate analgesia (paravertebral, serratus or erector spinae blocks or catheters), and a team learning curve that the trial's experienced centres had already climbed.

item.title: ESOT Bucharest consensus sets 130 rules for NRP in DCD donation: clamp, divide and vent the arch vessels
item.description:
Transpl Int · Consensus · 2026-07-22

Thirty-one experts from nine countries reached 75% agreement on 130 statements covering when to use abdominal and thoraco-abdominal normothermic regional perfusion and how to run it; they could not agree on a maximum warm ischemia time or whether arch vessels must be transected.

Take-home

  • TA-NRP brain exclusion: clamp or ligate the arch vessels, divide the cephalic ends and drain to atmosphere; ligation alone is not enough
  • Minimum team of five: cannulating clinician plus assistant, perfusionist, scrub and circulating nurses, coordinator; new teams work supervised
  • Blood gas at 3-4 minutes then every 30; avoid hyperoxemia, transfusion excess and cardiac distension; the heart comes out first

Why it matters. NRP is spreading faster than agreement on how to do it. The OPTN safety notice of November 2025 told US teams to transect and vent each arch vessel; this European consensus from the ESOT International DCD Congress in Bucharest is the most detailed attempt yet to write down the whole procedure. Published in Transplant International on 22 July 2026 (Minambres, first author; Cillo, corresponding), it anchors a five-paper special issue on controlled DCD.

What they did. Thirty-one experts from nine countries completed two Delphi rounds with 75% agreement as the threshold. Consensus landed on 130 statements.

What they agreed.

  • Machine perfusion should be routine in cDCDD; NRP is recommended after withdrawal of life support, especially with long expected warm ischemia or a higher-risk donor.
  • For TA-NRP, clamping or ligating the arch vessels plus dividing their cephalic ends and draining to atmospheric pressure excludes brain perfusion; ligation alone does not. No consensus on mandatory transection. Transcranial Doppler is not required; a written abort plan is.
  • TA-NRP needs a hybrid open ECMO circuit with a rigid reservoir and a pre-withdrawal CT (or arch dissection); A-NRP needs the descending aorta clamped first. Pre-withdrawal peripheral cannulation is acceptable for TA-NRP, not A-NRP.
  • Heparin and antemortem guidewires where the law allows; balanced crystalloid plus heparin in the prime; gases at 3-4 minutes then every 30; avoid hyperoxemia, transfusion excess and cardiac distension.
  • Assess the heart with a PA catheter, TEE or a brief volume load. If it cannot carry the circulation, clamp the thoracic aorta and run 2.0-2.4 L/min for the abdominal organs. Order: heart, liver, lungs, then pancreas and kidneys.

Left open. Maximum warm ischemia time, hypoperfusion thresholds, ideal NRP duration (typically 1-2 hours) and a case number for competence.

item.title: RATE: low-dose heparin or therapeutic LMWH is noninferior to standard heparin on ECMO, with no excess clotting
item.description:
Lancet · RCT · 2026-07-07

In a seven-centre Dutch open-label trial of 320 adults on VV or VA ECMO, low-dose unfractionated heparin (aPTT 1.5-2.0 times baseline) and twice-daily therapeutic LMWH were both noninferior to standard-dose heparin (aPTT 2.0-2.5 times) for a composite of severe bleeding, severe thromboembolism or death at 6 months.

Take-home

  • Composite of severe bleeding, thromboembolism or 6-month death: 81% standard UFH, 72% low-dose UFH, 75% LMWH
  • Severe thromboembolism was 9-11% in every arm; bleeding and mortality trended lower with less anticoagulation
  • Lower-intensity anticoagulation is a defensible default for ECMO patients without a separate indication for full dosing

Why it matters. Bleeding is the commonest serious complication of ECMO, and most units still run heparin to an aPTT of 1.5-2.5 times baseline on habit rather than trial data. Observational series hinted that less heparin bleeds less without more clotting. RATE is the first adequately sized randomised test.

What they did. Seven Dutch mixed ICUs randomised 330 adults on VV (40%) or VA (60%) ECMO between 2020 and 2024 to standard-dose UFH (aPTT 2.0-2.5 times baseline, roughly 60-75 s), low-dose UFH (1.5-2.0 times, roughly 45-60 s) or weight-adjusted therapeutic LMWH twice daily. Patients with a compelling indication for full anticoagulation, known PE or intracardiac thrombus, or HIT were excluded. The primary outcome was a net composite of severe bleeding or severe thromboembolism during ECMO, or death by 6 months, with a 7.5 percentage-point noninferiority margin; 320 were analysed.

What they found.

  • Composite: 81% standard, 72% low-dose UFH (difference -9.1%, 95% CI -20.3 to 2.1), 75% LMWH (-6.1%, -17.2 to 5.0). Both met noninferiority.
  • Severe bleeding 65% vs 58% vs 59%; severe thromboembolism 11% vs 10% vs 9%.
  • Six-month mortality 50% vs 42% vs 44%. Oxygenator exchanges were fewer with LMWH, and costs were lower in both intervention arms.
  • Exploratory VV subgroup: mortality 23% with low-dose UFH vs 46% with standard.

Caveats. Open label, event rates far above the 60-70% assumed, 13-28% crossover, and anti-Xa was measured in only 71 patients. Superiority was not shown for any outcome.

For the anaesthesiologist. Turning heparin down to an aPTT of 1.5-2.0 times baseline, or using LMWH when renal function allows, is now the evidence-based default for most adult ECMO runs. Keep full dosing for mechanical valves, known thrombus or active PE, and stay alert for the bleeding that still hit six in ten patients.

item.title: Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure: rigid LVEF cut-offs dropped for reduced, preserved and improved EF
item.description:
Circulation · Consensus · 2026-06-29

AHA, ACC, ESC and the World Heart Federation, with HFSA, HFA and the Japanese Heart Failure Society, updated the 2021 universal definition: HF phenotypes are grouped as reduced, preserved and improved ejection fraction without fixed numeric thresholds, a universal classification of causes is proposed, and improvement, remission and recovery trajectories are defined.

Take-home

  • Three EF groups replace the four-tier scheme; the mildly reduced category disappears, as in the 2026 ESC guideline
  • Stages A to D are retained, with Stage 0 for no risk factors; pre-HF (Stage B) keeps its emphasis on prevention
  • A universal etiological classification (ischaemic, infective, inflammatory and others) is proposed for records and trials

Why it matters. The 2021 universal definition gave us HFmrEF, HFimpEF and the pre-heart failure stage; every echo report, trial eligibility list and pre-op note has used that vocabulary since. The second edition, published in Circulation on 29 June 2026 and co-published in JACC (Walsh and colleagues), changes the vocabulary again.

What they did. A writing group convened by the AHA, ACC, ESC and World Heart Federation, in collaboration with HFSA, the HFA of the ESC and the Japanese Heart Failure Society, revised the 2021 document to standardise terminology for clinicians, researchers, health systems and policymakers and, in their words, to better reflect clinical reality.

What changed.

  • Phenotypes move away from rigid LVEF cut-offs and are grouped as reduced, preserved and improved ejection fraction; the mildly reduced category is gone, matching the 2026 ESC heart failure guideline published in August.
  • Staging keeps A (at risk), B (pre-HF), C (HF) and D (advanced HF), adds Stage 0 for people without risk factors, and sharpens the criteria for each stage.
  • A universal classification of causes is proposed, grouping for example ischaemic, infective (viral, Chagas, HIV) and inflammatory (sarcoid, autoimmune, desmoplakin) cardiomyopathies, to standardise registries and trials.
  • Trajectories of improvement, remission and recovery are defined, and the document addresses social determinants and geographic variation in HF risk and outcomes.

Caveats. A definition document, not a treatment guideline; numeric EF thresholds will persist in device and drug labels and in trial criteria for years, so expect a period of dual language.

For the anaesthesiologist. Update pre-operative templates and TEE reports: HFmrEF is leaving the lexicon, improved EF is a formal phenotype that still carries risk, and the cause of the cardiomyopathy should be named using the new taxonomy.

item.title: ADQI/ELSO consensus on kidney support during ECMO: CRRT when medical management fails, return blood pre-oxygenator
item.description:
Intensive Care Med · Consensus · 2026-05-06

The 36th ADQI meeting, held with ELSO in June 2025, produced 44 consensus statements across all ages on AKI epidemiology, fluid management, CRRT indications and delivery, biomarkers and drug dosing during ECMO (Gist and colleagues, Intensive Care Medicine, online 6 May 2026).

Take-home

  • AKI affects 50-70% of ECMO patients and about half receive CRRT; diagnose with KDIGO and treat modifiable risks
  • Start RRT when medical management fails fluid or metabolic goals, usually for fluid accumulation; ECMO itself is not an indication
  • Integrated CRRT returns blood before the membrane lung; avoid the pre-pump side because of air entrainment; remove fluid gradually

Why it matters. Half of adult ECMO patients end up on CRRT, and how the filter is plumbed into the circuit, when it starts and how fast fluid comes off are decided bed by bed. This is the first joint ADQI/ELSO document.

What they did. The 36th ADQI consensus conference met with ELSO in June 2025 with five working groups: epidemiology and outcomes; fluid management; indications for RRT and fluid removal; CRRT delivery; and biomarkers, blood purification and pharmacokinetics. A modified Delphi required over 80% agreement (over 90% for every final statement) on 44 statements spanning neonates to adults. Recommendations are deliberately ungraded.

Key statements.

  • Diagnose AKI by KDIGO; it occurs in 50-70% of ECMO patients and tracks with worse short- and long-term outcomes.
  • Fluid accumulation is associated with harm; aim for euvolaemia with individualised, dynamic removal targets, because brisk ultrafiltration drops venous return and compromises circuit flow.
  • RRT is indicated when medical management fails to meet fluid or metabolic goals and delay would be harmful; continuous modalities are preferred; no trial has tested early versus late initiation on ECMO.
  • Configuration: a pre-existing dialysis catheter can run a separate circuit; otherwise an in-line haemofilter or integrated CRRT device. Return blood before the membrane lung, which traps air and clots; the negative-pressure pre-pump side is reserved for cases where nothing else is practical, with bubble sensors.
  • Drug handling changes with AKI, circuit sequestration and haemodilution; use therapeutic drug monitoring more often.

Caveats. Opinion-based wherever trials are absent, which is most places; the statement count is reported inconsistently in the text.

For us. A single reference for perfusionists, intensivists and nephrologists to write one CRRT-on-ECMO protocol from, with the research agenda (timing, fluid strategy, dosing) spelled out.

item.title: HFA heart transplant consensus: DCD hearts now standard, machine perfusion beats cold storage, ECMO bridge fares worst
item.description:
Eur J Heart Fail · Consensus · 2026-05-05

The Heart Failure Association's Advanced Heart Failure Committee refreshed its heart transplant consensus in the European Journal of Heart Failure: candidate thresholds, donor expansion with DCD and ex vivo perfusion, bridging strategies and management of early graft failure.

Take-home

  • One-year survival by bridge: ECMO 71%, percutaneous VAD 80%, temporary BiVAD 86%, temporary LVAD 90%; durable LVAD bridging does not hurt survival
  • Candidacy: VO2max 12 or less (14 off beta-blockers), VE/VCO2 slope over 35; PVR over 3 WU, BMI over 35, GFR under 30
  • Early graft failure: inotropes first, temporary MCS if severe; peripheral VA-ECMO needs LV venting; pace the atrium above 90

Why it matters. Heart transplantation has changed quickly: DCD donors, ex vivo perfusion, and a waiting list where at least half the patients are bridged on a device. The HFA's Advanced Heart Failure Committee (Milicic, first author) updated its consensus in the European Journal of Heart Failure on 5 May 2026.

Donors. DCD hearts are called a clinical reality with excellent early outcomes, not inferior to brain-dead donors, with the potential to raise volume by about 50% where DCD donation is common. Ex vivo machine perfusion is preferred over static cold storage, and stable hypothermic preservation lowers primary graft dysfunction. Coronary angiography is advised for donors over 50 or with multiple risk factors; donors with unexplained encephalitis or unexplained arrest are excluded. A predicted heart mass ratio at or below 0.80 is linked to worse outcomes. NRP is not addressed.

Candidates. Contraindications are cumulative rather than absolute: persistent severe post-capillary pulmonary hypertension (PVR above 3 Wood units, tested for reversibility at catheterization), BMI above 35, GFR persistently below 30 mL/min, active substance abuse, recent cancer. Exercise thresholds: VO2max at or below 12 mL/kg/min (14 off beta-blockers) or VE/VCO2 slope above 35. PRA above 10% prompts a crossmatch.

Bridging. One-year survival by strategy: ECMO 71.2%, percutaneous VAD 79.9%, temporary BiVAD 86.2%, temporary LVAD 89.5%. Durable LVAD bridging gives post-transplant survival comparable to no bridge, with allosensitization screened. LVAD infection, recurrent pump thrombosis, recurrent GI bleeding, severe RV failure or refractory ventricular arrhythmia justify urgent listing; endocarditis or mediastinitis must resolve first.

Early graft failure. Recognize it fast, start inotropes, escalate to temporary MCS if severe. For RV failure: inotropes, inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin, preload optimization and atrial pacing above 90. Peripheral VA-ECMO cannot unload the LV, so add a left atrial cannula or a percutaneous VAD; VADs allow longer support.

item.title: Vasopressin after cardiac surgery: no change in 30-day kidney events or death in 3,753 vasopressor-dependent patients
item.description:
J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth · Observational · 2026-04-08

In a four-ICU Queensland cohort of adults needing at least six hours of vasopressors after cardiac surgery, adding vasopressin within 24 hours was not associated with major adverse kidney events at 30 days (OR 1.02) or with mortality, though the sickest tertile showed a trend toward benefit.

Take-home

  • Routine vasopressin for post-bypass vasoplegia does not appear to protect the kidney; pick it for pressure, not renal rescue.
  • Neutral for AKI (OR 1.04), new dialysis (OR 1.19) and 30-day death (OR 1.12) after overlap weighting.
  • Significant interaction with illness severity (p = 0.004) keeps the door open for the sickest patients.

Why it matters. Since the VANCS trial suggested vasopressin might reduce kidney injury and atrial fibrillation compared with norepinephrine in vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery, many units reach for it early. Whether that renal benefit holds in everyday practice has been unclear.

What they did. Multicentre retrospective cohort from four ICUs in the Queensland Critical Care Research Network, 2015-2021. Adults admitted after CABG, valve or combined surgery who needed at least six consecutive hours of vasopressor support in the first 24 hours were included; ECMO patients were excluded. Exposure was vasopressin within 24 hours of ICU admission. Inverse probability of treatment weighting with overlap weights balanced the groups.

What they found.

  • 3,753 patients; 603 (16.1%) received vasopressin
  • Primary outcome, major adverse kidney events at 30 days (death, new renal replacement therapy or creatinine doubling): OR 1.02 (95% CI 0.76-1.38, p = 0.88)
  • 30-day mortality OR 1.12 (0.69-1.82); AKI within 7 days OR 1.04 (0.85-1.28); new renal replacement therapy OR 1.19 (0.80-1.76)
  • Effect modification by illness severity (interaction p = 0.004), with a trend toward benefit in the highest-severity tertile

Caveats. Observational, with confounding by indication that weighting can only partly address; vasopressin dose, timing relative to shock onset and catecholamine exposure were not randomised. Four ICUs in one Australian network limit generalisability, and the severity subgroup finding is hypothesis-generating.

For the anaesthesiologist. Use vasopressin to restore pressure and spare catecholamines when that is the problem, not as a kidney-protective strategy. The sickest-tertile signal is the question a prospective trial should answer. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(7):2112-2121.

item.title: French shock guideline: norepinephrine first, dobutamine or milrinone next, Impella CP 'probably' in AMI shock
item.description:
Ann Intensive Care · Guideline · 2026-04-01

SRLF, the French Society of Cardiology, SFAR and the cardiac surgeons issue 41 GRADE recommendations on adult cardiogenic shock in Annals of Intensive Care, with Impella CP endorsed after a shock-team discussion in AMI shock and VA-ECMO reserved for selected deteriorating patients.

Take-home

  • Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor (Grade 1+); dopamine only if nothing else exists (1-); epinephrine probably not, except as rescue
  • Inotropes probably yes, dobutamine or milrinone first with no preference between them; epinephrine probably not as an inotrope
  • IABP not routine in AMI or heart failure shock (Grade 1-), except bridging mechanical complications; Impella CP 'probably' in AMI shock

Why it matters. After DanGer Shock, ECLS-SHOCK and the 2026 ESC heart failure guideline, every country is rewriting its shock pathway. This French document, from the Societe de Reanimation de Langue Francaise and the French Society of Cardiology with SFAR and the cardiovascular surgeons, appeared in Annals of Intensive Care (16:100038) in spring 2026 with Aissaoui and Delmas as co-first authors.

What they did. Twenty-three PICO questions across six fields, from shock teams to de-escalation. Output: 41 recommendations, 7 Grade 1, 11 Grade 2, 17 expert opinion, 6 unanswered, all with strong agreement.

Drugs.

  • Norepinephrine first (Grade 1+). Dopamine only when nothing else is available (1-). Epinephrine should probably not be used as vasopressor or inotrope (2-), with a last-resort caveat. Nothing on vasopressin or angiotensin II.
  • Inotropes should probably be used (2+), dobutamine or milrinone first with no preference between them.

Devices.

  • IABP: not routine in AMI shock or decompensated heart failure shock (both 1-); suggested as initial support for mechanical complications of infarction as a bridge to repair.
  • Impella CP should probably be considered in AMI shock after shock-team discussion (2+), with the DanGer Shock price of more bleeding, limb ischemia and sepsis noted; Impella 5+ is suggested for predominant LV failure (expert opinion).
  • VA-ECMO should probably not be used routinely in AMI shock (2-); consider it in selected deteriorating patients after shock-team discussion, and in selected bridge-to-transplant candidates. No position on MCS timing relative to PCI or on LV unloading.

Revascularization. Angiography as soon as feasible, culprit-lesion PCI as early as possible, non-culprit PCI staged (all 1+).

For the anesthesiologist. Nothing here contradicts the ESC line, which makes it a useful second reference when building a shock team: pressor and inotrope choices are explicit, and every device decision runs through the team.

item.title: SOFRIB: rib plating did not shorten ICU stay and tripled pneumonia, though pain and quality of life were better later
item.description:
Annals of Surgery · RCT · 2026-03-26

In a nine-centre US trial of 236 adults with three or more displaced rib fractures plus pulmonary compromise, severe pain or deformity, surgical stabilisation within 5 days versus standardised non-operative care did not change ICU length of stay (mean difference 1.8 days, P = 0.17), lengthened hospital stay by 3.3 days and raised pneumonia from 3.3% to 11.4%, while improving SF-36 pain and physical scores.

Take-home

  • Primary outcome ICU length of stay: no difference; hospital stay 3.3 days longer and pneumonia 11.4% vs 3.3% with fixation
  • SF-36 general health, bodily pain and physical component scores improved beyond the minimal clinically important difference
  • Supports selective fixation for flail chest and specific patterns; blocks, catheters and respiratory therapy remain the standard

Why it matters. Rib plating has spread well beyond flail chest on the strength of registry data, and the 2023 single-centre Annals trial had already shown longer hospital stays with fixation. SOFRIB is the largest multicentre randomised test, and it lands alongside the ACS chest wall injury guideline that put regional blocks on par with epidurals.

What they did. Ang and colleagues (Annals of Surgery, online 26 March 2026) randomised 236 adults at nine ACS-verified trauma centres between 2014 and 2024. Inclusion needed three or more displaced fractures plus pulmonary compromise, severe pain or chest wall deformity. Patients were allocated 1:1 to surgical stabilisation within 5 days (114) or standardised non-operative care (122); analysis was intention to treat and the primary outcome was ICU length of stay.

What they found.

  • ICU stay: mean difference 1.8 days, 95% CI -0.8 to 4.4, P = 0.17.
  • Hospital stay 3.3 days longer with fixation (P = 0.01); pneumonia 11.4% vs 3.3% (risk ratio 3.45, P = 0.02).
  • SF-36 general health +3.3, bodily pain +4.0 and physical component +3.3 points, each beyond the minimal clinically important difference; PIQ-6 pain impact lower by 3.9 points.
  • Return to work 62.5% vs 38.7%, not significant (P = 0.08).

Caveats. Ten years to enrol 236 patients at nine centres implies slow accrual and selection; analgesic regimens, surgical technique and timing varied; the patient-reported outcomes were secondary and unblinded.

For the anaesthesiologist. The acute-care case for routine plating is weaker than its advocates assumed, and the operated patient needs an anaesthetic and often a ventilator that the medically managed patient avoids. The lever you control, early catheter-based regional analgesia with aggressive pulmonary toilet, remains the standard against which fixation must prove itself. Reserve the operating room for flail segments and patients failing that care.

item.title: SVS 2026 blunt aortic injury: no repair for grades 1-2, delayed TEVAR for stable grade 3, emergent repair for grade 4
item.description:
J Vasc Surg · Guideline · 2026-03-24

The Society for Vascular Surgery's focused update of its 2011 guideline (DuBose and colleagues, writing group chaired by Azizzadeh) issues 13 recommendations: definitive non-operative management for minimal aortic injury, TEVAR after 24 hours for stable grade 3 injuries so other injuries can be treated first, urgent repair when the aorta is the cause of instability, and no anti-impulse therapy for grade 1-2 injuries with traumatic brain injury.

Take-home

  • Grade 1: no routine follow-up imaging; grade 2: one CTA to confirm resolution; neither gets TEVAR or open repair
  • Grade 3 stable: delayed TEVAR beyond 24 h; grade 3 unstable from the aorta: urgent or emergent; grade 4: emergent repair
  • With TBI or solid organ injury: no anti-impulse therapy for grades 1-2, individualised targets for grade 3, joint decision on heparin

Why it matters. Blunt thoracic aortic injury is among the leading causes of death after blunt trauma, and the anaesthesiologist is the one running the blood pressure between the CT scanner and the endovascular suite. The 2011 SVS guideline predates most of the TEVAR and grading literature.

What they did. DuBose, Azizzadeh and the SVS writing group (Journal of Vascular Surgery, online 24 March 2026; print May 2026) commissioned a systematic review and issued 13 updated recommendations using the SVS grade 1-4 injury scale.

What it says.

  • Grades 1 and 2 (minimal aortic injury): definitive non-operative management is recommended over TEVAR or open repair. Grade 1 needs no routine follow-up imaging; grade 2 gets a single follow-up CTA to confirm resolution.
  • Grade 3, haemodynamically stable: delayed TEVAR, beyond 24 hours, is suggested so that other injuries can be addressed first.
  • Grade 3 with instability attributable to the aorta: urgent (under 24 hours) or emergent intervention. Grade 4: emergent repair.
  • Grade 1-2 with traumatic brain injury: anti-impulse therapy is not recommended and blood pressure management should prioritise the brain. Grade 3 with TBI or solid organ injury: anti-impulse therapy and TEVAR timing are individualised with trauma surgery and neurosurgery.
  • Intraprocedural anticoagulation during TEVAR in patients with TBI or solid organ injury should be decided collaboratively.

Caveats. Evidence quality is low throughout and most recommendations are suggestions; left subclavian management, spinal drainage and numeric pressure targets are not covered in the summary material we could verify.

For the anaesthesiologist. The reflex beta-blocker infusion for every aortic injury on the CT report is gone for grades 1-2, and the patient with a concomitant head injury gets the neurosurgical pressure target. Build the heparin conversation into the pre-TEVAR huddle rather than at the moment of deployment.

item.title: Pediatric Surviving Sepsis 2026: 10-20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment, peripheral pressors early, no etomidate
item.description:
Pediatr Crit Care Med · Guideline · 2026-03-23

The children's Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline is rewritten for the first time since 2020: 68 experts from 13 organizations issued 61 statements, 20 of them new, and adopted the newer organ-dysfunction definition of pediatric sepsis.

Take-home

  • Septic shock with ICU access: up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour as 10-20 mL/kg boluses, reassessing after each one
  • Start vasoactives through a peripheral line rather than waiting for central access; no first-line pick between epinephrine and norepinephrine
  • Suggests against hydrocortisone once shock responds to fluid and pressors, and against etomidate for intubation

Why it matters. The adult Surviving Sepsis update landed in March 2026; this is the children's version, published online in Pediatric Critical Care Medicine on 23 March with an executive summary alongside (Weiss, first author). It comes from 68 experts across 13 organizations and adopts the newer definition of pediatric sepsis: infection plus life-threatening respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation or neurologic dysfunction.

What they produced. Sixty-one statements: 5 strong recommendations, 24 conditional, 10 good-practice statements, and 22 questions with no recommendation (7 carry an 'in our practice' note). Twenty recommendations are new, 13 updated, 6 unchanged, 22 carried forward. Only three rest on high or moderate certainty.

What they say.

  • Septic shock with ICU access: up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour as 10-20 mL/kg boluses, reassessing after each. Sepsis without hypotension and without ICU access: no boluses (strong, high certainty). Balanced crystalloid over saline; crystalloid over albumin.
  • Vasoactives through a peripheral line rather than delaying for central access. No verdict on epinephrine versus norepinephrine, or on pressors before 40 mL/kg. At high catecholamine doses, add vasopressin or keep titrating.
  • Suggests against hydrocortisone once shock is stabilized with fluid and vasoactives; stress-dose steroids still for suspected adrenal insufficiency.
  • Antimicrobials within 1 hour for suspected septic shock, within 3 hours for probable sepsis without shock. Measure lactate. Cardiac and lung POCUS to guide resuscitation where skills allow; target ScvO2 of 70% or more when a central line exists.
  • Suggests against etomidate for intubation; SpO2 88-92% after resuscitation; VV ECMO for refractory hypoxemia, VA ECMO only as rescue.

For the anesthesiologist. This is the playbook for the septic child who arrives for source control: modest boluses with reassessment, a peripheral pressor started early, no etomidate, and steroids only for adrenal insufficiency.

item.title: VATS lobectomy beats open surgery on survival in pooled randomised data: HR 0.79 for death, same disease-free survival
item.description:
Lancet · Meta-analysis · 2026-03-21

An individual patient data meta-analysis of the three randomised trials of VATS versus open lobectomy for early-stage NSCLC (Danish, Chinese and UK VIOLET; 1,185 patients) found a 21% lower hazard of death with VATS and similar disease-free survival, with no heterogeneity across trials.

Take-home

  • Overall survival HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65-0.96) for VATS; disease-free survival HR 0.91 (0.75-1.12)
  • Three trials, 586 VATS vs 599 open; result held after excluding benign disease
  • The oncological-equivalence worry is answered; thoracotomy now needs a technical justification

Why it matters. VATS became the default lobectomy approach for early-stage lung cancer because patients recover faster and hurt less, not because anyone had shown it was oncologically as good. Surgeons who favoured thoracotomy pointed out that no trial was powered for survival. This NIHR-funded pooled analysis (Harris, Lim and colleagues; Lancet 2026;407:1182-1190) closes that argument.

What they did. A systematic search through June 2025 found three randomised trials of VATS versus open lobectomy in early-stage NSCLC: the Danish trial of Bendixen (median follow-up 9.5 years), the Chinese trial of Long (5.2 years) and the UK VIOLET trial of Lim (3.8 years). Individual patient data for all 1,185 participants (586 VATS, 599 open) were pooled in a one-stage random-effects Cox model.

What they found.

  • Overall survival: HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.65-0.96), a 21% lower hazard of death with VATS, in the same direction in every trial.
  • Disease-free survival: HR 0.91 (0.75-1.12).
  • No statistical heterogeneity; excluding benign disease gave HR 0.78 for survival and 0.89 for disease-free survival.

Caveats. Three trials, modest total numbers, and VIOLET follow-up is still short. Because recurrence was not reduced, the survival gain presumably reflects fewer complications and better delivery of adjuvant therapy rather than a better cancer operation. Robotic approaches were not studied.

For the anaesthesiologist. Expect even fewer thoracotomies, and expect conversion to be a true emergency rather than a routine. The anaesthetic contribution to the survival advantage, faster extubation, less opioid and early mobilisation, is part of why minimally invasive surgery wins; the thoracotomy patient now needs the full PROSPECT analgesic package precisely because they are the exception.

item.title: In 1.16 million US CABG admissions, Black patients died in hospital at 3.2% vs 2.4%; the gap did not narrow in six years
item.description:
J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth · Registry · 2026-03-10

A National Inpatient Sample analysis of 1,159,040 isolated CABG hospitalisations found Black patients had higher in-hospital mortality (3.2% vs 2.4%, adjusted OR 1.22), two extra days in hospital and more cardiogenic shock and sepsis, with no narrowing of the gap across six years.

Take-home

  • Black CABG patients were younger (mean 63) but sicker (Charlson index 3.25 vs 2.52) and still died more often after adjustment.
  • Mortality trends were flat for every group (P-trend > 0.30): national quality programmes have not closed the gap.
  • Preoperative optimisation and shock recognition are the modifiable parts of this story for perioperative teams.

Why it matters. Equity in cardiac surgical outcomes has been a stated priority of surgical and anaesthesia societies for a decade. This is the largest contemporary national look at whether anything has changed after CABG, and the answer is no.

What they did. Retrospective cohort using the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project National Inpatient Sample, 2016-2021. Adults undergoing isolated CABG were grouped by race and ethnicity; multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic and clinical factors. Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes were length of stay, cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock and sepsis.

What they found.

  • 1,159,040 CABG hospitalisations; Black patients were 6.7% of cases
  • Black patients were younger (mean age 63) with a higher comorbidity burden (Charlson index 3.25 vs 2.52)
  • In-hospital mortality 3.2% vs 2.4% in the comparison group (adjusted OR 1.22, p < 0.01)
  • Length of stay 11.8 vs 9.6 days; more cardiogenic shock and sepsis
  • No significant improvement in mortality for any group over time (P-trend > 0.30)

Caveats. Administrative data rely on ICD coding without STS-style physiological risk variables, cannot separate hospital effects from patient effects fully, and capture only the index admission. Adjusted odds ratios describe association, not mechanism.

For the anaesthesiologist. The excess risk travels with comorbidity, later presentation and more shock, which are things a perioperative team can act on: anaemia and diabetes optimisation, earlier mechanical support decisions, and structured handover to the ICU. The paper is also the citation for anyone building an equity dashboard around cardiac surgical outcomes. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(7):2096-2102.

item.title: AAP policy: infants and complex children belong with fellowship-trained pediatric anesthesiologists in equipped centers
item.description:
Pediatrics · Guideline · 2026-02-23

The AAP Section on Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine updates its policy on the critical elements of a pediatric periprocedural anesthesia environment, published in Pediatrics (March 2026), with a companion clinical report on the pediatrician's role in preparing children for anesthesia.

Take-home

  • Anesthesiologist privileges should reflect fellowship training and ongoing case experience; high-risk children by age, comorbidity or procedure go to designated specialists
  • Facilities with neonatal and pediatric ICUs should have pediatric fellowship-trained anesthesiologists; PACU needs pediatric equipment, experienced nurses, respiratory therapy and child life
  • Required infrastructure spans preoperative evaluation, pediatric-ready ORs, lab, blood bank and radiology, an opioid stewardship program and anesthesia QI

Why it matters. Children under one year carry the highest risk of serious injury or death from anesthesia complications, and the question of which hospitals should anesthetize which children keeps surfacing in credentialing and in the ACS Children's Surgery Verification program. The AAP's Section on Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine (Long, Houck and Varughese, lead authors) has rewritten its policy, approved by the AAP board and released 23 February 2026 ahead of the March issue of Pediatrics (157:e2025075746). A companion clinical report, The Pediatrician's Role in the Evaluation and Preparation of Pediatric Patients Undergoing Anesthesia, appears in the same issue.

What it asks for.

  • Physician anesthesiologists whose privileges reflect fellowship training and enough ongoing experience to stay competent, and advanced practice providers with appropriate pediatric training.
  • Designation of high-risk patients, by age, comorbidity or procedure, to specialized anesthesiologists, with pediatric fellowship-trained anesthesiologists in facilities that run neonatal and pediatric intensive care units.
  • Pediatric-specific care across the pathway: preoperative evaluation and preparation, operating rooms, laboratory, blood bank, radiology, and pediatric equipment and drugs.
  • A PACU with age-appropriate equipment and experienced nursing, plus respiratory therapy and child life, and the capacity for postoperative inpatient care or a transfer partnership when complications arise.
  • An acute pain program that includes opioid stewardship, and an anesthesia quality improvement program.

Caveats. It is a policy statement, not a graded guideline; it sets no numeric staffing ratios and names no age cut-off beyond flagging infants under one year as highest risk.

For the anesthesiologist. The recommendations track the ACS CSV standards closely, which is no accident given the overlap in authorship. For anyone arguing for pediatric equipment, a dedicated PACU nurse or a transfer agreement, this is the citation.

item.title: 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline: 'massive' and 'submassive' are out, PERT is Class 1, deep sedation is Class 3 Harm
item.description:
Circulation · Guideline · 2026-02-19

The first joint AHA/ACC clinical practice guideline on acute PE in adults, written with CHEST, SCAI, SIR and six other societies, replaces risk tiers with clinical categories A to E, makes PE response teams Class 1 for categories C to E, and warns against intubation and deep sedation unless unavoidable.

Take-home

  • Categories A-E are set by the most severe finding; E1 is persistent hypotension or shock, E2 refractory shock or arrest
  • Systemic lysis: Class 3 Harm through C2, may be considered in D, reasonable in E; VA-ECMO is the E2 alternative
  • If a category C-E patient must be intubated, have VA-ECMO at the bedside and use the gentlest induction you can

Why it matters. Anaesthesiologists meet PE at its worst: the intraoperative collapse, the arrest on induction, the ECMO call from the cath lab. This is the first full AHA/ACC clinical practice guideline, co-written with ACCP, ACEP, CHEST, SCAI, SHM, SIR, SVM and SVN (Creager, chair; Circulation, online 19 February 2026).

What changed.

  • Massive, submassive and low-risk are replaced by categories A (subclinical) through E (cardiopulmonary failure), assigned by the most severe indicator. C splits into C1-C3 by RV dysfunction and biomarkers, D is incipient failure such as normotensive shock, E1 is persistent hypotension or cardiogenic shock, E2 refractory shock or arrest.
  • Categories C to E are admitted with troponin or BNP, lactate and echo of the RV; a PE response team is Class 1.
  • Anticoagulation: DOACs over warfarin and LMWH over UFH (both Class 1); no routine IVC filters in anticoagulated patients (Class 3 Harm).
  • Systemic thrombolysis is Class 3 Harm through C2, may be considered in D1-D2 and is reasonable in E. Catheter-directed lysis or mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in D and is reasonable in E1. Surgical embolectomy is reasonable in E1 but not preferred over VA-ECMO in E2.
  • Deep sedation and mechanical ventilation are Class 3 Harm in categories C to E unless clinically necessary; norepinephrine is first line, dobutamine for low output, and VA-ECMO should be ready if intubation is unavoidable.

Caveats. Many interventional recommendations rest on registry and single-arm data; the category scheme is new and needs validation; the document covers adults only.

For us. Learn the letters, because consults will use them. The explicit warnings about induction and positive pressure in a failing RV, and the instruction to have ECMO available before intubating a category C-E patient, are the lines to put in your department's PE pathway.

item.title: International fasting consensus: encourage clear fluids until 2 h, allow 'sip til send' by protocol, gum until transfer
item.description:
Anaesthesia · Consensus · 2026-02-09

A 68-stakeholder, three-round Delphi across five continents, including patients, nurses, surgeons and anaesthetists, agreed eight recommendations: keep the 6-hour solid rule, actively encourage clear liquids until 2 hours before anaesthesia, let institutions permit more liberal intake, and resume oral intake as soon as feasible.

Take-home

  • Clear liquids should be encouraged, not merely permitted, until 2 h before anaesthesia or sedation
  • Institutions may adopt more liberal protocols such as sipping until called; solids stay at 6 h, longer for heavy meals
  • Chewing gum and sweets allowed until transfer; a trained operator's gastric ultrasound can settle doubtful cases

Why it matters. Patients routinely fast for 10-14 hours because instructions are conservative and lists slip. Prolonged fasting from clear fluids worsens thirst, hypotension at induction, glucose handling and recovery, with no evidence of fewer aspirations. National guidelines had drifted apart, and UK 'sip til send' programmes had moved ahead of them.

What they did. Ruggeberg and colleagues (Anaesthesia, online 9 February 2026) ran a systematic review, drafted 13 recommendations and put them through three Delphi rounds with 68 stakeholders: patients, anaesthetists, surgeons, physicians, nurses and representatives of international organisations from five continents. Eight recommendations survived.

What they agreed.

  • Clear liquids (water, tea or coffee with a little milk, pulp-free juice, clear carbohydrate drinks) should be actively encouraged until 2 hours before the start of anaesthesia or sedation, unless an institutional protocol permits more liberal intake, such as sipping until called to the procedure room.
  • Solids and non-clear liquids keep the 6-hour rule, longer after large or fatty meals; nothing solid within 2 hours.
  • Salivation stimulants such as chewing gum and lollipops may continue until transfer and restart in recovery.
  • Oral intake should resume as soon as clinically feasible after the procedure.
  • Pre-procedural gastric ultrasound by a trained provider may inform decisions when more information is needed.

Caveats. Consensus, not trial evidence; adults only; it does not replace drug-specific guidance such as the multisociety advice on GLP-1 receptor agonists. Liberal regimens are meant to run inside written institutional protocols, not ad hoc.

For the anaesthesiologist. The direction of travel is settled: the default is a drink two hours before, not nil by mouth from midnight. Writing the local protocol, including who decides on the delayed case and when to scan the stomach, is now the job.

item.title: ASE/EACVI strain consensus endorses GLS, RV free-wall and LA reservoir strain; radial and regional strain are not
item.description:
Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Imaging · Consensus · 2026-01-30

The first joint ASE/EACVI document devoted to clinical strain (Thomas, chair), published in JASE in November 2025 and in EHJ-Cardiovascular Imaging on 30 January 2026, grades every strain measure by indication and standardizes acquisition and reporting.

Take-home

  • LV GLS endorsed for cardio-oncology and valve-disease prognosis; report end-systolic strain with the negative sign and quote vendor-specific normals
  • RV free-wall strain endorsed in MI, heart failure, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension; use the RV-focused apical view and dedicated RV software
  • Radial strain and regional strain are not endorsed; no randomized trial has tested strain-guided decisions, so the grades are expert opinion

Why it matters. Strain has lived in guidelines piecemeal since 2015, with vendors, views and cut-offs that never quite lined up. This is the first joint ASE/EACVI document devoted to its clinical use, published in JASE in November 2025 and in European Heart Journal - Cardiovascular Imaging (27:335-368) on 30 January 2026.

What they did. The writing group graded each measure, by indication, as clinically endorsed (+++), may be appropriate (++), or not currently endorsed, and set out technical standards and pitfalls. No large randomized trial has tested strain-based decisions, so the grades are expert opinion.

What is endorsed.

  • LV GLS as a complementary measure of global function, reported as end-systolic longitudinal strain with the negative sign kept; lower limits of normal differ slightly by vendor. It gets +++ for diagnosis and prognosis in cardio-oncology and for prognosis in at least moderate valve disease.
  • RV free-wall longitudinal strain is +++ for diagnosis and prognosis in acute and chronic MI, heart failure, undifferentiated cardiomyopathy, CRT, athlete's heart and pulmonary hypertension, and ++ in adult congenital disease and stress echo. Use the RV-focused apical four-chamber view, because the standard view underestimates, and dedicated RV software rather than repurposed LV software.
  • LA reservoir strain is +++ in undifferentiated cardiomyopathy and acute and chronic heart failure, ++ in most other settings, and not endorsed in adult congenital disease.

What is not. Radial strain is not endorsed. Regional strain is not supported because of variability, though curve shape can help. Midwall or full-wall tracking is preferred; speckle tracking for chamber-wide assessment, tissue Doppler for a single region.

For the perioperative echo reader. RV free-wall strain and GLS now carry society backing for the RV-failure and valve-disease questions that precede LVAD and valve surgery, provided you use the right view and software.

item.title: SCA and STS publish the first joint consensus on managing DOACs before, during and after cardiac surgery
item.description:
Anesthesia & Analgesia · Consensus · 2026-01-29

The Society of Cardiovascular Anesthesiologists and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons issued a joint consensus statement on patients taking factor Xa or direct thrombin inhibitors who need cardiac surgery, built on a systematic review plus expert consensus, published in Anesthesia & Analgesia (online 29 January 2026, April 2026 issue) and co-published in the Annals of Thoracic Surgery.

Take-home

  • Five domains: when to stop the DOAC, how to check residual drug activity, whether to bridge, how to reverse, when to restart.
  • Summary statements pair the evidence with expert consensus for each domain, written for anesthesiologists and surgeons together.
  • Use it to rebuild your pre-admission DOAC protocol, assay access and emergency reversal pathway; read the full text for specifics.

Why it matters. A large share of patients arriving for CABG, valve or aortic surgery are on apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran, and the questions come up every week: how many days to hold, whether a drug level is worth sending, what to do when surgery cannot wait, which reversal agent to reach for, and when the surgeon is comfortable restarting. Practice has varied by institution and by who was on call. European surgeons issued recommendations in 2023; this is the first joint statement from the two US societies that share these patients.

What they did. Budd, Kertai, Wyler von Ballmoos, Raphael, Ghadimi and colleagues, writing for the SCA and the STS, ran a systematic review of the literature on stopping DOACs before cardiac surgery, monitoring options, the need for bridging, reversal agents, and resuming anticoagulation after surgery, then completed a structured expert consensus process. The output is a set of summary statements for each domain, each tied to the evidence and the panel's agreement.

What it covers.

  • Preoperative cessation, including how renal function and drug choice change the timing.
  • Measuring residual effect, and where calibrated assays help when timing is uncertain or surgery is urgent.
  • Bridging, which the statement addresses directly rather than leaving to habit.
  • Reversal strategies for emergent and bleeding patients, including the specific reversal agents and prothrombin complex concentrate.
  • Postoperative resumption in a way both specialties can sign off on.

Caveats. Much of the base is observational, so several statements rest on consensus rather than trial data, and the document is a guide rather than an hour-by-hour mandate; the full text carries the specifics this summary deliberately does not paraphrase.

For the anesthesiologist. This is the document to cite when you standardize the DOAC questions in pre-admission testing, secure anti-Xa and dabigatran assays with a quick turnaround, agree a reversal pathway with pharmacy and blood bank, and set a resumption plan with your surgeons.

item.title: Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS 2026: proceed with elective surgery below 180/120 in clinic; home readings now count
item.description:
Anaesthesia · Guideline · 2026-01-14

The planned update of the 2016 UK blood pressure guideline, built by Delphi, tells hospitals to accept referrals with a documented clinic BP under 160/100 (or home or ambulatory under 155/95) in the past year, and to proceed at pre-assessment if the clinic reading is under 180/120 or the out-of-office reading under 175/115.

Take-home

  • Referral accepted with clinic BP under 160/100, or ambulatory/home under 155/95, documented within 12 months
  • No primary-care record: proceed if clinic BP is under 180/120 or home/ambulatory under 175/115
  • Scope is adults having planned non-cardiothoracic, non-obstetric, non-endocrine surgery, decision to operate to 30 days after

Why it matters. A raised blood pressure on the morning of surgery is still one of the commonest reasons for a cancelled list, even though the link between pre-operative hypertension and perioperative harm is weak below very high values. The 2016 Association of Anaesthetists and British Hypertension Society guideline set a clinic cut-off of 180/110 mmHg; this is the planned update, now with the British and Irish Hypertension Society (McCormack and colleagues, Anaesthesia, online 14 January 2026).

What they did. An expert working party ran a targeted literature review and a modified Delphi process. Scope: adults having planned surgery other than cardiothoracic, obstetric or endocrine procedures, from the decision to operate to 30 days after surgery.

What it says.

  • Secondary care should accept a referral that documents a clinic BP below 160/100 mmHg, or an ambulatory or home BP below 155/95 mmHg, within 12 months.
  • A patient arriving at pre-operative assessment without a documented primary-care reading may proceed if the clinic BP is below 180/120 mmHg, or an out-of-office reading is below 175/115 mmHg.
  • Out-of-office measurement is given equal standing with clinic readings, and the document covers measurement, referral back to primary care and perioperative management.
  • A short companion paper from the same group (Frank and colleagues, Anaesthesia, online 19 March 2026) addresses which antihypertensives to continue or hold.

Caveats. Consensus-based and UK-focused; the thresholds are about proceeding safely, not about intraoperative targets, which still rest on the individual patient's baseline. Cardiac surgery is explicitly out of scope.

For the anaesthesiologist. Fewer same-day cancellations for isolated readings in the 160-180 systolic range, a defined role for home monitoring, and a clear message that long-term control belongs to primary care rather than to the pre-op clinic.

item.title: AHA standardizes right heart cath protocols: LVAD ramp targets CVP under 12, PAWP under 18, CI over 2.2
item.description:
Circ Heart Fail · Consensus · 2026-01-06

An AHA scientific statement (Belkin, chair) sets common protocols for baseline, provocative and serial invasive hemodynamics in heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, including vasoreactivity testing before transplant, fluid and exercise challenges, LVAD ramp studies and when a PA catheter earns its place.

Take-home

  • Pre-transplant PH reversibility: test with nitroprusside or a milrinone bolus, inhaled NO if PAWP is not elevated; PH predicts 30-day post-transplant death
  • Maglev LVAD optimization: invasive ramp and reverse-ramp studies over echo alone, aiming for CVP under 12, PAWP under 18, CI over 2.2
  • Continuous PAC monitoring endorsed for advanced PH or RV dysfunction in high-risk procedures, LVAD implant, pulmonary endarterectomy and POPH liver transplant

Why it matters. Right heart catheterization numbers drive transplant listing, LVAD settings and the liver transplant go or no-go in portopulmonary hypertension, yet protocols vary from lab to lab. This AHA statement, in Circulation: Heart Failure (19:e000088) in January 2026 with Belkin as chair and Fudim as vice chair, sets common ground for static, provocative and serial measurements in heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, LVAD patients and cardiogenic shock.

What it says.

  • Pre-transplant: pulmonary hypertension predicts 30-day mortality after heart transplant. Test reversibility with sodium nitroprusside or a milrinone bolus; inhaled nitric oxide can be used when wedge pressure is not elevated.
  • Occult post-capillary PH: when resting numbers do not explain dyspnea, a fluid bolus or passive leg raise can unmask it. Invasive exercise testing identifies the cause of exertional symptoms; exercise-induced PH predicts outcome but is not yet a treatment target.
  • Acute vasoreactivity testing in suspected idiopathic, heritable or drug-induced PAH: inhaled prostacyclin analogs or NO preferred; a positive response is a fall in mean PA pressure of 10 mm Hg or more to below 40 mm Hg without a drop in cardiac output.
  • Magnetically levitated LVADs: invasive ramp and reverse-ramp studies are preferred over echo alone, targeting CVP under 12 mm Hg, PAWP under 18 mm Hg and cardiac index above 2.2 L/min/m2, which track with fewer admissions and hemocompatibility events.
  • Continuous PA catheter monitoring is useful in advanced PH or RV dysfunction during high-risk procedures, LVAD implantation, pulmonary endarterectomy and liver transplantation with portopulmonary hypertension; routine early PAC use in cardiogenic shock still needs data.

For the anesthesiologist. This is the reference for the pre-transplant vasodilator study, the LVAD ramp you are asked to supervise, and the argument for a PA catheter in the POPH liver transplant.

item.title: EACTAIC issues its first consensus on monitoring in thoracic anaesthesia, from basic monitors to NMB and brain
item.description:
J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth · Consensus · 2025-12-18

A 45-author EACTAIC task force has published consensus recommendations on what to monitor during thoracic anaesthesia, covering respiratory, circulatory, neuromuscular and neurological monitoring in routine and specialised settings. It is the first of a series of thoracic consensus documents.

Take-home

  • First European consensus on monitoring for thoracic cases; use it to audit your lung-resection and OLV monitoring bundle.
  • Recommendations are graded by agreement level: agreed (>60%), strong (>80%) and full (>95%) consensus.
  • Authors stress the evidence base is thin, so treat this as a shared baseline rather than a rulebook.

Why it matters. Thoracic anaesthesia has lacked a society document on which monitors belong in the room, when advanced haemodynamic or neuromonitoring is worth it, and how to interpret it during one-lung ventilation. EACTAIC's Thoracic Subcommittee has now published the first of a planned series of consensus documents, written by its General Management: Monitoring Task Force.

What they did. Senior thoracic anaesthesiologists from Europe, the United States, Africa and the Middle East (45 named authors) reviewed the evidence and voted on statements. Agreement is reported in three tiers: agreed (more than 60%), strong (more than 80%) and, for some statements, full consensus (more than 95%).

What it covers.

  • Standard basic and advanced monitoring for thoracic patients
  • Respiratory and circulatory monitoring in routine and specialised settings
  • Monitoring of neuromuscular blockade, depth of anaesthesia and neurological function
  • Research priorities, and how monitoring links to good clinical practice and enhanced recovery after lung surgery

Caveats. The authors are candid that high-level evidence is limited and that controversies remain; the document consolidates diverse practice rather than settling it. Nothing here is a randomised result, and some statements reached only the lowest consensus tier.

For the anaesthesiologist. This is the reference to cite when standardising a thoracic monitoring bundle, deciding on arterial and central access, or arguing for quantitative neuromuscular and depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring in a lung-resection pathway. Read it alongside the companion EACTAIC airway document published in the same month. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(3):985-993.

item.title: EACTAIC airway consensus for thoracic anaesthesia: lung isolation goals, DLT practice, blockers and the difficult airway
item.description:
J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth · Consensus · 2025-12-05

EACTAIC's Airway Management Task Force has published a consensus document on lung isolation and separation, comparing double-lumen tubes and bronchial blockers in routine and difficult airways and answering six clinical questions. It is the third document in the society's thoracic consensus series.

Take-home

  • Covers goals of lung isolation, best practice for double-lumen tubes, the role of bronchial blockers and difficult-airway plans.
  • Statements graded by agreement: agreed (>60%), strong (>80%), full (>95%); evidence base is acknowledged as limited.
  • Useful template for a departmental lung-isolation protocol and for teaching trainees the device trade-offs.

Why it matters. Lung isolation is the defining skill of thoracic anaesthesia, yet choices between double-lumen tubes and bronchial blockers, and plans for the patient with both a difficult airway and a need for one-lung ventilation, have mostly rested on local habit. This EACTAIC document gives the subspecialty a shared reference.

What they did. The Airway Management Task Force of the EACTAIC Thoracic Subcommittee (around 40 authors, the TOSSCA Consensus Group) reviewed the evidence and had senior clinicians from Europe, the United States, Africa and the Middle East evaluate the statements. Consensus is reported as agreed (more than 60%), strong (more than 80%) and, in places, full (more than 95%).

What it covers. Six clinical questions:

  • The goals of lung isolation and the means of achieving separation
  • Best practice for double-lumen tubes
  • The role of bronchial blockers
  • Management of the difficult airway in thoracic surgery
  • Special cases
  • Research priorities

It compares the benefits and drawbacks of each device in routine and difficult scenarios and ties the recommendations to good clinical practice and enhanced recovery.

Caveats. As with the monitoring document, the authors state that high-level evidence is generally limited and that significant controversies remain. The abstract does not give a count of recommendations, and some statements sit at the lowest agreement tier.

For the anaesthesiologist. Use it to standardise device selection and sizing, to write the difficult-airway-plus-OLV algorithm every thoracic unit should have on the wall, and as the citation when a surgeon asks why a blocker was chosen. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(4):1276-1287.

item.title: DESIGNATION: driving pressure-guided PEEP plus recruitment did not cut pulmonary complications after abdominal surgery
item.description:
JAMA · RCT · 2025-12-03

Across 29 European sites, 1,435 adults at increased pulmonary risk having open abdominal surgery were randomised to individualised PEEP titrated to the lowest driving pressure plus recruitment manoeuvres, or fixed PEEP 5 without recruitment; the composite of pulmonary complications within 5 days was 19.8% vs 17.4%.

Take-home

  • Postoperative pulmonary complications 19.8% vs 17.4% (difference 2.5%, 95% CI -1.5 to 6.4); hospital mortality 3.6% vs 3.3%
  • High PEEP caused more hypotension (54% vs 45%) and vasopressor use (32% vs 19%), with less desaturation (0.8% vs 2.8%)
  • With PROTHOR in thoracic surgery, that is two large trials: tidal volume 8 mL/kg, PEEP 5, no routine recruitment

Why it matters. After PROVHILO and iPROVE, the individualised ventilation camp argued that PEEP should be titrated to each patient's mechanics using driving pressure rather than set high or low for everyone. DESIGNATION, from the PROVE Network, is the definitive test of that idea in open abdominal surgery, and it reported three weeks after PROTHOR delivered the same verdict for one-lung ventilation.

What they did. Investigator-initiated trial at 29 sites in five European countries, April 2019 to December 2024. Adults with ARISCAT 26 or higher and BMI up to 40 having open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia were randomised to volume-controlled ventilation at 8 mL/kg predicted body weight with either a recruitment manoeuvre followed by decremental PEEP titration to the lowest driving pressure (default 12 cmH2O), repeated at set points including before extubation, or fixed PEEP 5 cmH2O with no recruitment. Outcome assessors were blinded; 1,435 patients were analysed.

What they found.

  • Composite of pulmonary complications within 5 days: 19.8% vs 17.4%, absolute difference 2.5% (95% CI -1.5 to 6.4; P = 0.23).
  • Intraoperative hypotension 54.0% vs 45.0%; vasoactive drug use 32.0% vs 18.8%.
  • Desaturation 0.8% vs 2.8%; unplanned ICU admission 1.3% vs 2.5% (not significant); hospital mortality 3.6% vs 3.3%.
  • Patients already planned for ICU or HDU had more complications with high PEEP (33.9% vs 23.6%, interaction P = 0.007), a hypothesis-generating signal.

Caveats. Event rates were below the planning assumptions, so the interval does not exclude a small benefit or harm; clinicians could not be blinded; the comparator was already lung-protective.

For the anaesthesiologist. Better mechanics and oxygenation on the monitor did not translate into fewer complications and cost more pressors. Low tidal volume with PEEP 5 remains the default; individualised PEEP is for rescue of the hypoxaemic patient, not routine.

item.title: ERS/ESTS replace the 2009 lung resection fitness algorithm: DLCO for everyone, ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO under 40% is high risk
item.description:
Eur Respir J · Guideline · 2025-11-13

The first full rewrite of the ERS/ESTS fitness guideline, co-published in ERJ and EJCTS and endorsed by ESAIC, makes DLCO a strong recommendation for every surgical candidate, calls for routine predicted postoperative values, and sets field-test and CPET thresholds.

Take-home

  • DLCO in every surgical candidate; ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO calculated routinely, with under 40% high risk and 40-59% moderate
  • One field test screens: walk over 400 m or stair climb over 10 m suggests low risk; poor performers go to CPET
  • CPET: VO2peak under 12 mL/kg/min or VE/VCO2 slope over 40 flags high risk; repeat FEV1 and DLCO after neoadjuvant therapy

Why it matters. The 2009 ERS/ESTS algorithm has decided who is offered a lung resection for 16 years. This replacement, chaired by Brunelli, Hardavella and Huber, was co-published in the European Respiratory Journal (66:2500156) and the European Journal of Cardio-Thoracic Surgery in November 2025 and endorsed by ESAIC, ESTRO and IASLC. Its scope now covers radiotherapy and systemic treatment as well as surgery, plus nutrition, frailty, prehabilitation and sublobar resection.

What they did. A multidisciplinary panel with patient representatives answered four PICO and seven narrative questions with GRADE and an evidence-to-decision framework.

What changed.

  • DLCO for every surgical candidate is now a strong recommendation, and ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO should be calculated routinely rather than only when spirometry is impaired. Bands: DLCO 60-79% mild, 40-59% moderate, under 40% high; ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO under 40% high, 40-59% moderate.
  • Repeat FEV1 and DLCO after neoadjuvant therapy; post-induction DLCO or ppo values under 80% signal higher risk.
  • One low-technology test screens exercise capacity: a 6-minute or shuttle walk above 400 m or a stair climb above 10 m suggests low risk, and poor performers are referred for CPET.
  • CPET: VO2peak below 12 mL/kg/min or a VE/VCO2 slope above 40 suggests high surgical risk, with no single parameter mandated.
  • Do not select on a risk score alone (EuroLung 2 is for benchmarking). Assess nutrition when BMI is under 18.5, weight loss is 10% or more, or age is over 70; screen frailty after 60. Prehabilitation can reduce pulmonary complications in high-risk patients (moderate certainty). Offer smoking cessation. Age alone should not decide treatment.

For the anesthesiologist. Expect ppo values and a field test in every thoracic clinic note, and expect to anesthetize patients the 2009 rules would have declined, now with prehabilitation and sublobar options on the table.

item.title: Delirium is coded after 1 in 20 US CABGs and rising; it nearly doubles in-hospital death and adds 4 days and $8,565
item.description:
J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth · Registry · 2025-11-12

In 911,910 isolated CABG admissions from the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2021), coded postoperative delirium occurred in 4.9% and rose each year. Delirium carried an adjusted 1.85-fold higher in-hospital mortality, four extra days in hospital and $8,565 in added cost.

Take-home

  • Dementia (aOR 4.28), alcohol misuse (3.38) and psychotic disorders (2.40) flag the highest-risk CABG patients before induction.
  • Coded delirium is rising about 4% a year; expect the true screened incidence to be several times higher.
  • Cost and length-of-stay numbers are useful ammunition for funding a delirium prevention bundle.

Why it matters. Delirium after cardiac surgery is common, but national-scale numbers on trend, risk and cost have been scarce. This NIS analysis gives anaesthesiologists citable figures for prevention programmes and for the preoperative conversation with high-risk patients.

What they did. Retrospective analysis of the US National Inpatient Sample, 2016-2021, using discharge weights. Adults with isolated CABG were identified, and postoperative delirium was defined by validated ICD-10 codes. Multivariable models adjusted for patient and hospital factors.

What they found.

  • 911,910 weighted CABG hospitalisations; delirium coded in 4.91%
  • Incidence rose over the period (OR 1.04 per year, p < 0.001)
  • Strongest independent predictors: pre-existing dementia (aOR 4.28), alcohol abuse (aOR 3.38), psychotic disorders (aOR 2.40)
  • Delirium was independently associated with in-hospital death (aOR 1.85), more major complications, a 4-day longer stay and $8,565 higher cost (all p < 0.001)

Caveats. Administrative coding under-detects delirium: prospective screening studies after cardiac surgery report far higher rates, so the 4.9% is a floor, and the rising trend may partly reflect better documentation. Associations with mortality are adjusted but not causal, and the dataset lacks STS-style physiological risk variables, anaesthetic technique and sedation data.

For the anaesthesiologist. The risk-factor profile is actionable at the preoperative visit: cognitive screening, alcohol history and psychiatric medication review identify who needs the full delirium bundle (avoid benzodiazepines, multimodal analgesia, early mobilisation, sleep protection). The cost figure makes the business case. Print version: J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2026;40(2):561-570.

item.title: ELSO issues a dedicated narrative guideline on ECMO for pregnant and peripartum patients
item.description:
ASAIO J · Guideline · 2025-11-01

An international ELSO writing group led by Erika O'Neil, with Emily Naoum, Marc Anders, Kollengode Ramanathan and Matteo Di Nardo, publishes ELSO's guidance on extracorporeal support of pregnant and recently delivered patients in the November 2025 ASAIO Journal.

Take-home

  • One ELSO reference now exists for peripartum ECMO; read it before the next amniotic fluid embolism or peripartum cardiomyopathy arrives
  • A narrative guideline: structured expert guidance on practices ELSO considers useful and safe, not a GRADE document or standard of care
  • Same issue carries ELSO's accidental hypothermia guideline; both were released by ELSO in October 2025

Why it matters. Peripartum collapse is where obstetric and cardiac anesthesia meet: amniotic fluid embolism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, massive hemorrhage with arrest, and severe ARDS in a patient whose physiology, airway, anticoagulation and fetus all complicate the usual ECMO rules. Until now ELSO had no guideline specific to pregnancy. This narrative guideline fills that gap, published in ASAIO Journal 71(11):875-887 (November 2025, online 24 September 2025) by an international writing group led by Erika O'Neil, with Ahmed Labib Shehatta, Cara Agerstrand, Caroline Sampson, Farah Siddiqui, Priya Nair, Alexandra Schou, Javier Kattan, Emily Naoum, Marc Anders, Kollengode Ramanathan and Matteo Di Nardo.

What it is. ELSO's narrative guidelines are structured expert documents rather than GRADE-graded recommendations. ELSO describes them as educational, built on practices it believes are useful and safe, based on the data available when written, and due for revision as evidence accrues; they explicitly do not guarantee an outcome or define a standard of care.

What to do with it. Use it to build the pathway before the case rather than during it: who cannulates and where, which configuration, how anticoagulation and bleeding risk are weighed against the uterus and the surgical field, and how delivery is planned around the circuit. A short list of named roles, the multidisciplinary call tree, and a stocked cannulation cart on the labor floor are the kind of practical steps a document like this is meant to prompt.

Caveat. The full text sits behind the ASAIO Journal paywall; this post rests on the citation, the author list and the guideline's stated scope, not on a line-by-line read. Pull the PDF through your library before writing local protocol from it.
